analysis.body:
# AI Data Center Demand Signals in the US Grid Queues

As of early September 2026, commercial electricity sales across eight major states totaled 54,798 megawatt-hours in June, with Texas consuming the largest share at 15,754 MWh—nearly three times California's 10,025 MWh. Prices tell a different story: California's commercial rate of $27.33 per megawatt-hour far exceeds Texas at $8.66, while Virginia and Georgia offer rates under $11. Since data centers are billed largely within the commercial sector, these sales volumes and price gradients suggest where computational workloads are concentrating and where expansion economics most favor new facilities.

The five major grid interconnection queues show 8,364 projects totaling 1.33 million megawatts of planned generation and storage capacity. ERCOT's Texas queue dominates with 438,086 MW across 1,778 requests, followed by NYISO at 319,095 MW and MISO at 299,721 MW. These queues track supply waiting to connect, not data center demand directly, but their fuel composition signals what infrastructure developers expect will power future loads: across all five regions, solar leads with roughly 279,000 MW of requests, while battery storage alone represents over 328,000 MW—a combination particularly suited to smoothing data center power patterns.

Gas capacity in the queues—totaling approximately 184,509 MW—remains substantial across all regions, with ERCOT and SPP each requesting over 47,000 MW of new gas generation. The growth in both storage and gas alongside high commercial electricity sales in data-center-dense states suggests developers are hedging against both peak demand and renewable variability. Monitor next month's queue updates to track whether project withdrawals accelerate or if new requests concentrate further in lower-cost regions like Texas, which would signal where capital is actually flowing.
